pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of DECK)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of deck, from Dutch dekken (to cover, adorn), formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Deckedst thy high places with divers colours, and playedst the harlot thereupon. Paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments.

Deckedst appears twice, both times in Ezekiel's oracles against Jerusalem and Samaria under the figure of an adulterous wife, and both times the adorning is an act of betrayal rather than beauty rightly used. The first oracle pictures Jerusalem taking the very garments the LORD gave her and using them to deck her high places with divers colours, turning gifts of covenant love into decoration for idol-shrines. The second, addressed to the sister-figure Aholibah, pictures the same self-adorning aimed outward, toward foreign lovers sent for from far off: thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments, all the outward motions of a bride preparing to meet her husband, performed instead to meet strangers. In both scenes, decking is not condemned as such — the tabernacle itself is richly adorned at God's own command — but decking turned from its rightful object to a rival becomes, in Ezekiel's unsparing figure, the very picture of spiritual adultery.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DECK: to cover; to array; to adorn, dress, or embellish; here in the archaic second-person singular past, deckedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: DECK, v.t. To cover; to overspread.
DECK, v.t. To dress with elegance; to array; to adorn; to embellish.
DECKEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as paintedst.
In Ezekiel 16 the word names Jerusalem decking her high places with the LORD's own gifts.
In Ezekiel 23 the same word names Aholibah decking herself to meet foreign lovers.
scriptures: And of thy garments thou didst take, and deckedst thy high places with divers colours, and playedst the harlot thereupon: the like things shall not come, neither shall it be so.

And furthermore, that ye have sent for men to come from far, unto whom a messenger was sent; and, lo, they came: for whom thou didst wash thyself, paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments,
corruption_summary: Modern readings embarrassed by Ezekiel's marital and bodily imagery often minimize deckedst as mere ancient color, missing that the oracle's entire force depends on adornment itself being turned from its rightful covenant use to serve idols and foreign alliances.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading uncomfortable with the sexual bluntness of Ezekiel 16 and 23 can pass quickly over deckedst thyself with ornaments as incidental detail rather than the oracle's central charge — a bride's own preparations, meant for her husband, redirected to strangers. The specificity (garments, colours, painted eyes, ornaments) is deliberate: this is not vague infidelity but itemized betrayal.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that adornment itself is not the sin in either oracle — the tabernacle and its priests are richly decked at God's own command elsewhere in the Law — the sin is adornment redirected from covenant love to rival gods and rival nations.
roots_summary: Deckedst appears only in Ezekiel's twin oracles against Jerusalem and Samaria under the marriage figure, the word's two occurrences bracketing the whole indictment of covenant unfaithfulness pictured as harlotry.
roots_lines: Deckedst in Ezekiel 16 names Jerusalem using the LORD's own gifts to adorn idol high places.
The same verse pairs deckedst with playedst the harlot, decoration turned to idolatry.
Deckedst in Ezekiel 23 names Aholibah preparing herself to meet foreign lovers sent for from far.
Both oracles use bridal preparation imagery — washing, painting, adorning — to picture betrayal.
The prophets' marriage figure for covenant unfaithfulness runs throughout Hosea, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel alike.
usage: Deckedst thy high places with divers colours, and playedst the harlot thereupon — gifts turned to idolatry.
Paintedst thy eyes, and deckedst thyself with ornaments — bridal preparation redirected to strangers.
For whom thou didst wash thyself — the deliberate, itemized nature of the betrayal Ezekiel names.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of DESIRE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of desire, formed with the -edst ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
According to all that thou desiredst of the LORD thy God in Horeb. O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me.

Desiredst names two requests answered in opposite ways. Moses recalls Israel's own request at Horeb, that thou desiredst of the LORD thy God, when the people, overwhelmed by the fire and thunder of the law given, asked not to hear the LORD's voice directly again — a desire the LORD himself called right, and answered by raising up a prophet like Moses to mediate his word from then on (Deut 18:17-18). Christ's parable turns the same word toward mercy: I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me, the king's forgiveness of an impossible debt granted entirely on the strength of a servant's desperate request, with no ability on the servant's part to repay. Desiredst thus marks the hinge on which both a nation's ongoing relationship with God and one man's eternal debt turn — not on merit, but on the request itself, made and answered.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DESIRE: to wish for; to long for the possession or enjoyment of; here in the archaic second-person singular past, desiredst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: DESIRE, v.t. To wish for the possession or enjoyment of, with a degree of earnestness.
DESIRE, v.t. To request; to express a wish for.
DESIREDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -edst, as intendest.
In Deuteronomy 18 the word names Israel's request not to hear God's voice directly at Horeb.
In Matthew 18 the same word names a servant's desperate plea, met with total forgiveness of debt.
scriptures: According to all that thou desiredst of the LORD thy God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not.
Then his lord, after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me:
corruption_summary: Reading the parable of the unmerciful servant as a lesson primarily about interpersonal etiquette, rather than about the total, undeserved forgiveness that must produce a forgiving heart, misses the parable's own hinge word — because thou desiredst me, mercy granted purely on request, with no merit attached.
corruption_paragraphs: A moralized reading of Matthew 18 can reduce the parable to generic advice about being nice to others, losing the specific weight of because thou desiredst me — the king's forgiveness rests entirely on the servant's plea, not on any repayment plan or partial merit, an impossible debt (ten thousand talents) cancelled outright. The servant's later cruelty to his fellow servant is damnable precisely because he received what he could never have earned.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Deuteronomy 18's own pattern: Israel's desire at Horeb not to hear God directly is not rebuked as unbelief but honored — that thou hast well spoken, saith the LORD (Deut 18:17) — and answered by the provision of a mediating prophet, the pattern that finds its fulfillment in Christ.
roots_summary: The two occurrences of desiredst frame the word at opposite ends of covenant history: a nation's request for a mediator at Sinai, and a single debtor's request for mercy in Christ's own parable, both requests answered by grace rather than refused as presumption.
roots_lines: Desiredst in Deuteronomy 18 recalls Israel's own request not to hear God's voice directly at Horeb.
The LORD calls that request right, and answers it by promising a prophet like Moses to mediate his word.
Desiredst in Matthew 18 names a servant's plea for mercy, granted as total cancellation of an impossible debt.
The servant's later refusal to forgive a much smaller debt condemns him out of his own request.
Both occurrences show a desire honestly voiced being met with grace rather than being refused.
usage: According to all that thou desiredst of the LORD thy God in Horeb — Israel's request for a mediator.
Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God — the specific desire Moses recalls and God honors.
I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me — mercy granted purely on request, in Christ's parable.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of KILL)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of kill, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian? When the LORD had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not.

Killedst names one act of violence and, in its second occurrence, a violence deliberately withheld. The Hebrew man in Egypt who confronts Moses the day after his killing of the Egyptian taskmaster throws the deed back in Moses' face — as thou killedst the Egyptian — exposing a sin Moses thought hidden and driving him into forty years of exile before the LORD calls him at the burning bush. David's use of the same word is its precise inversion: standing over a sleeping, vulnerable Saul in the cave at Engedi, David refuses the killing his men urge, and Saul himself is forced to confess it afterward — when the LORD had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not. One occurrence exposes a killing that happened; the other confesses a killing that, though fully within reach, did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from KILL: to deprive of life; to put to death; here in the archaic second-person singular past, killedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: KILL, v.t. To deprive of life; to put to death, in any manner.
KILL, v.t. To destroy; to put an end to.
KILLEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as feltest, feltest.
In Exodus 2 the word exposes Moses' killing of the Egyptian taskmaster, previously thought hidden.
In 1 Samuel 24 the same word confesses a killing deliberately withheld by David from Saul.
scriptures: Exo 2:14
And he said, Who made thee a prince and a judge over us? intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian? And Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known.
And thou hast shewed this day how that thou hast dealt well with me: forasmuch as when the LORD had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not.
corruption_summary: Reading Moses' killing of the Egyptian as heroic proto-liberation activism, rather than as the very sin Exodus itself exposes and that sends Moses into forty years of humbling exile, inverts the text's own verdict on premature, self-appointed deliverance.
corruption_paragraphs: Some readings admire Moses' violence against the Egyptian taskmaster as an early act of justified resistance, skipping past that Exodus itself frames it as a sin Moses tries to hide (looked this way and that way, Exo 2:12), a killing his own countryman throws back at him in reproach, and the direct cause of a forty-year exile before the LORD calls Moses to deliver Israel by his own word and power, not Moses' premature violence.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is David's own restraint at Engedi: thou killedst me not is Saul's forced confession of an enemy's mercy, and it stands as Scripture's own commendation of trusting God's timing for vindication rather than seizing it by force, even when the opportunity and the provocation are both real.
roots_summary: The two occurrences of killedst stand a full biblical era apart — the Exodus's earliest chapters and the era of David's flight from Saul — yet together frame the same lesson from opposite sides: killing seized is exposed and judged, killing withheld is commended and confessed.
roots_lines: Killedst in Exodus 2 exposes Moses' hidden killing of an Egyptian taskmaster, sin rather than heroism.
The exposure drives Moses into forty years of exile before the LORD calls him at the burning bush.
Killedst in 1 Samuel 24 is Saul's own confession that David spared his life when he could have taken it.
David's restraint at Engedi becomes one of Scripture's clearest models of trusting God's timing over force.
Both occurrences involve a life fully within another's power, one ended, one deliberately preserved.
usage: Intendest thou to kill me, as thou killedst the Egyptian — Moses' hidden sin exposed by his own countryman.
And Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known — the exposure that sends Moses into exile.
When the LORD had delivered me into thine hand, thou killedst me not — Saul's confession of David's mercy.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of LOVE)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of love, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version.
biblical_def:
Thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it. For thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.

Lovedst names love given to two utterly different objects. Isaiah's oracle against Judah's idolatry uses the word for a love turned toward false gods pictured as illicit lovers: thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it, a nation's affection given away to what it should never have desired, adultery again the prophets' chosen figure for covenant betrayal. Christ's high-priestly prayer uses the identical archaic form for a love of an entirely different order, spoken to the Father about the Son: thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world, love within the eternal Trinity itself, prior to and independent of creation, the ground from which the Son's own prayer for his people's future glory proceeds. Set side by side, the two occurrences mark the widest possible span of biblical love — misdirected covenant affection judged as idolatry, and the eternal love of the Father for the Son that is the very source and pattern of the gospel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LOVE: to have a strong affection for; to regard with tender attachment; here in the archaic second-person singular past, lovedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: LOVE, v.t. To have a strong attachment of the heart to.
LOVE, v.t. To regard with tender affection, as that of male and female, or of friend and friend.
LOVEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as sawest.
In Isaiah 57 the word names Judah's idolatrous love, a covenant affection misdirected.
In John 17 the same word names the Father's eternal love for the Son, before creation itself.
scriptures: Isa 57:8

Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance: for thou hast discovered thyself to another than me, and art gone up; thou hast enlarged thy bed, and made thee a covenant with them; thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it.
Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
corruption_summary: Open Theist and process-theology readings that make divine love contingent on, or developing alongside, creation cannot account for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world — the Father's love for the Son in John 17 is eternal and prior to creation, not a love that begins or grows with time.
corruption_paragraphs: A theology that treats God's love as something that unfolds or increases through relationship with the created order, rather than as eternally complete within the Trinity itself, has no place for before the foundation of the world. Christ's own prayer grounds the disciples' future glory not in anything creation supplies to God, but in a love that already existed in full before there was a world to love within.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own warning alongside John's comfort: thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it shows covenant love, once given rightly to the LORD, can be catastrophically misdirected — the same capacity for love that should rest in the eternal Father-Son relation is exactly what idolatry corrupts and steals away.
roots_summary: The two occurrences of lovedst stand at the extremes of biblical theology, one naming creaturely love catastrophically misdirected toward idols, the other naming the uncreated love within the Godhead itself, the same archaic verb form carrying both without strain.
roots_lines: Lovedst in Isaiah 57 names Judah's idolatrous affection, pictured under the figure of adultery.
The oracle catalogs specific acts — enlarging the bed, making a covenant with false gods — as evidence.
Lovedst in John 17 names the Father's love for the Son, existing before the foundation of the world.
Christ's prayer grounds the disciples' future glory in this eternal love, not in anything creation adds to it.
The same word thus spans idolatry's counterfeit love and the Trinity's own eternal, uncreated love.
usage: Thou lovedst their bed where thou sawest it — Isaiah's oracle against Judah's idolatrous affection.
Thou hast made thee a covenant with them — covenant language turned toward false gods, not the LORD.
Thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world — the Father's eternal love for the Son in Christ's prayer.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of OBEY)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of obey, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version — appearing only in oracles that pronounce judgment for a specific disobedience.
biblical_def:
Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the LORD, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek. This hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice.

Obeyedst appears twice, and both times names disobedience rather than obedience, the negative always attached. Samuel's word to Saul, delivered through the witch of Endor on the very night before his death, traces the whole of Saul's coming ruin back to a single, specific failure years earlier: because thou obeyedst not the voice of the LORD, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, the incomplete obedience of 1 Samuel 15 named again as the hinge of the kingdom's loss. Jeremiah's oracle against Judah's king widens the charge from one act to a whole life's pattern: this hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice, a lifetime's disobedience summarized in one sentence of judgment. Both occurrences testify that partial obedience, to God, is simply disobedience under another name — Saul's careful preservation of the best of the sheep and oxen was not called caution but rebellion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from OBEY: to comply with the commands of; to submit to the direction or control of; here in the archaic second-person singular past, obeyedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: OBEY, v.t. To comply with the commands, orders, or instructions of; to submit to the government of.
OBEY, v.t. To yield submission to; to be ruled by.
OBEYEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as executedst.
In 1 Samuel 28 the word traces Saul's coming death back to his disobedience regarding Amalek.
In Jeremiah 22 the same word summarizes a king's entire lifetime pattern of disobedience.
scriptures: Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the LORD, nor executedst his fierce wrath upon Amalek, therefore hath the LORD done this thing unto thee this day.
I spake unto thee in thy prosperity; but thou saidst, I will not hear. This hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice.
corruption_summary: Reading Saul's failure regarding Amalek as excessive severity on God's part, rather than as the exposure of partial obedience as real disobedience, softens 1 Samuel's own verdict that to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22).
corruption_paragraphs: A modern sensibility uncomfortable with the total judgment commanded against Amalek can sympathize with Saul's partial compliance — sparing Agag and the best of the flocks — as reasonable moderation rather than rebellion. Samuel's own verdict, spoken to Saul's face in chapter 15 and recalled again through the witch of Endor in chapter 28, names it plainly as rebellion... and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry (1 Sam 15:23), obeyedst not standing for a real, specific, costly refusal.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own wider lens: this hath been thy manner from thy youth shows that a single disobedience, left unrepented, becomes a settled pattern — Saul's one incomplete obedience and Jehoiakim's lifelong refusal are the same root sin at different stages of growth.
roots_summary: Both occurrences of obeyedst are spoken in judgment rather than commendation, and both trace present ruin back to a specific, nameable refusal to obey — Amalek in Saul's case, a whole reign in Jehoiakim's — rather than to vague or general fault.
roots_lines: Obeyedst in 1 Samuel 28 traces Saul's coming death to his incomplete obedience regarding Amalek.
The word is spoken by Samuel's spirit through the witch of Endor, the night before Saul's own death.
Obeyedst in Jeremiah 22 widens the charge from a single act to a king's whole lifetime pattern.
This hath been thy manner from thy youth names disobedience as a settled habit, not an isolated lapse.
Both occurrences deny that partial or occasional obedience counts as obedience before the LORD.
usage: Because thou obeyedst not the voice of the LORD... upon Amalek — Saul's ruin traced to a specific refusal.
Therefore hath the LORD done this thing unto thee this day — judgment spoken the night before Saul's death.
This hath been thy manner from thy youth, that thou obeyedst not my voice — a lifetime pattern named.

pos: v. (archaic 2nd pers. sing. past, of TESTIFY)
etymology: Archaic second-person singular past tense of testify, formed with the -st ending used with thou throughout the Authorized Version, appearing twice in successive verses of Nehemiah's great covenant prayer.
biblical_def:
Testifiedst against them, that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law. Testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets: yet would they not give ear.

Testifiedst is Nehemiah's word for God's own patient, repeated warning across the whole of Israel's history, spoken twice within two verses to underline how long-suffering that patience was. The first occurrence names the purpose of God's testifying — that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law — discipline always aimed at restoration, never mere punishment for its own sake. The second widens the timeframe: yet many years didst thou forbear them, and testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets, the entire prophetic office summarized as one long testimony against a people who would not give ear. The prayer's own conclusion is severe and just at once — therefore gavest thou them into the hand of the people of the lands — exile finally following not a sudden divine impatience but many years of testifying refused.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TESTIFY: to bear witness; to give solemn testimony in confirmation of a fact; here in the archaic second-person singular past, testifiedst, addressed to thou.
webster_full: TESTIFY, v.i. To bear witness; to make a solemn declaration of fact.
TESTIFY, v.t. To affirm or declare solemnly, as before a witness or under oath.
TESTIFIEDST, the archaic second-person singular past, formed with -st, as forbearest.
Both occurrences appear in Nehemiah 9, the Levites' great covenant-renewal prayer.
The word names God's own prophetic warning, given repeatedly across Israel's history.
scriptures: Neh 9:29

And testifiedst against them, that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law: yet they dealt proudly, and hearkened not unto thy commandments, but sinned against thy judgments, (which if a man do, he shall live in them;) and withdrew the shoulder, and hardened their neck, and would not hear.
Neh 9:30
Yet many years didst thou forbear them, and testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets: yet would they not give ear: therefore gavest thou them into the hand of the people of the lands.
corruption_summary: Reading the exile as capricious or disproportionate divine anger, rather than as judgment following many years of patient testifying refused, ignores the prayer's own emphasis on the LORD's forbearance before the sentence finally fell.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading that isolates gavest thou them into the hand of the people of the lands from the two preceding verses can treat the exile as sudden or excessive. Nehemiah 9 explicitly frames it otherwise: many years didst thou forbear them precedes the judgment, and testifiedst is doubled in successive verses specifically to underline how long and how patiently the warning was repeated before it was finally executed.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is verse 29's own stated purpose behind every testimony: that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law — even God's warnings of judgment are, in their intention, acts of covenant mercy aimed at restoration, not mere retribution, however finally that mercy is refused.
roots_summary: The doubled use of testifiedst within two consecutive verses is itself a feature of Nehemiah 9's prayer style, which repeatedly stacks near-synonymous verbs (forbear, testify, hearken not, give ear) to build a cumulative case for the LORD's patience against Israel's persistent refusal.
roots_lines: Testifiedst in Nehemiah 9:29 names God's warning aimed at bringing Israel back to the law, not mere punishment.
The same verse lists Israel's response: dealt proudly, hardened their neck, would not hear.
Testifiedst in Nehemiah 9:30 widens the warning to the entire prophetic office across many years.
The prayer explicitly notes many years of forbearance before the sentence of exile was carried out.
The doubled verb across two verses builds the prayer's case for the LORD's patience, not his impatience.
usage: Testifiedst against them, that thou mightest bring them again unto thy law — warning aimed at restoration.
Yet many years didst thou forbear them — the LORD's patience emphasized before judgment falls.
Testifiedst against them by thy spirit in thy prophets — the whole prophetic office as one long testimony.

etymology: Latin evidens (clearly seen, obvious), from e- (out) + videre (to see) — that which is placed plainly before the eyes, admitting no reasonable doubt.
biblical_def:
He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day an angel of God. Before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you.

Evidently in the Authorized Version names something made unmistakably plain, not a vague impression but a clear, undeniable perception. Cornelius's vision comes to him evidently, at a fixed hour of prayer, with an angel's instruction precise enough to send named men to a named house in a named city — nothing hazy about it, and the narrative's careful detail underlines that this was real revelation, not a devout man's wishful imagining. Paul's rebuke of the Galatians turns the same word toward the preached gospel itself: before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you, Paul's own preaching described as having made the cross as plain and unmistakable to the Galatians' understanding as Cornelius's vision was to his own eyes. Both uses insist that God does not deal in vagueness — neither in the visions he sends nor in the gospel he commands preached.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from EVIDENT: clear to the mind; obvious; manifest to the senses or understanding, admitting no reasonable doubt.
webster_full: EVIDENT, a. Plain, clear, manifest to the mind; open to be seen.
EVIDENTLY, adv. Clearly; plainly; in a manner to be certainly and clearly known.
Used of Cornelius's vision, received with unmistakable clarity as to time, content, and instruction.
Used of Paul's gospel preaching to the Galatians, described as having made Christ's cross plainly visible.
In both cases the word rules out vagueness, ambiguity, or mere subjective impression.
scriptures: Act 10:3
He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day an angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius.
Gal 3:1
O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you, that ye should not obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you?
corruption_summary: Reading Cornelius's vision or Paul's preaching as ambiguous religious experience open to any interpretation contradicts the text's own repeated insistence on evidently — clear, specific, unmistakable communication, not vague spiritual impression.
corruption_paragraphs: A subjectivist approach to religious experience treats every vision or conviction as equally valid and inherently ambiguous, resistant to clear content or verification. Luke's careful narration of Cornelius's vision — the hour, the angel's words, the instruction to send to a named man in a named house — is the opposite of ambiguous; it is evidently, checkable, specific revelation, later confirmed independently by Peter's own vision and the Spirit's descent on Cornelius's household.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's own rebuke in Galatians: a gospel evidently set forth, plainly preached, leaves no excuse for being bewitched away from it by a different gospel, however sophisticated its arguments.
roots_summary: Evidently shares its Latin root videre (to see) with evidence, providence, and vision itself, the family of words built on clear sight standing behind Scripture's own preference for plain, verifiable revelation over vague impression.
roots_lines: Evidently in Acts 10 describes Cornelius's vision as precise in time, content, and instruction.
The vision's specificity is later confirmed independently by Peter's own vision and the Spirit's descent.
Evidently in Galatians 3 describes Paul's own preaching of Christ crucified among the Galatians.
Paul's rebuke assumes the Galatians once understood the gospel plainly before being bewitched from it.
Both occurrences oppose evidently to vagueness, ambiguity, or merely subjective religious feeling.
usage: He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day — Cornelius's precise, specific revelation.
An angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius — content as clear as the vision's timing.
Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth, crucified among you — the plainness of Paul's own gospel preaching.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon scearp (sharp) + -ly — an edge-word applied figuratively to speech that cuts rather than soothes, used in the Authorized Version of rebuke rightly given.
biblical_def:
They did chide with him sharply. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith.

Sharply names a hard word spoken for a good end, in two very different situations. The men of Ephraim, aggrieved at being left out of Gideon's campaign against Midian, did chide with him sharply — a sharpness born of wounded pride, which Gideon answers not in kind but with a soft answer that turns away wrath (Prov 15:1), his own restraint contrasted with their sharpness. Paul's instruction to Titus commends a different sharpness altogether, aimed not at defending one's own honor but at the health of the church: rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, false teachers on Crete confronted plainly because their error, left unaddressed, would corrupt whole households. Scripture thus distinguishes sharpness that merely wounds pride from sharpness that heals doctrine — the same word naming a fault in Ephraim's men and a pastoral duty in Titus.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHARP: cutting, keen; applied figuratively to speech that is severe, biting, or pointed rather than gentle.
webster_full: SHARP, a. Having a fine edge or point; keen.
SHARP, a. Severe; harsh; biting, as words or reproof.
SHARPLY, adv. In a sharp manner; severely; keenly; vehemently.
In Judges 8 the word describes Ephraim's aggrieved chiding of Gideon, born of wounded pride.
In Titus 1 the same word describes Paul's pastoral instruction to rebuke false teachers plainly.
scriptures: Jdg 8:1
And the men of Ephraim said unto him, Why hast thou served us thus, that thou calledst us not, when thou wentest to fight with the Midianites? And they did chide with him sharply.
Tit 1:13
This witness is true. Wherefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith;
corruption_summary: Therapy-culture instinct treats any sharp rebuke as inherently unloving or spiritually abusive; Paul's own instruction to Titus commands sharp rebuke precisely so that false teachers and those they deceive may be sound in the faith, the sharpness itself an act of pastoral love, not its opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: A conflict-averse church culture that treats all firm correction as harmful reads rebuke them sharply as an embarrassing relic rather than binding pastoral instruction. Paul's stated purpose removes any ambiguity: that they may be sound in the faith — the sharpness is medicinal, aimed at spiritual health, applied specifically to those deceiving whole houses (Tit 1:11) for dishonest gain, not to ordinary believers in ordinary disagreement.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Gideon's own contrasting example: Ephraim's sharpness, born of wounded pride over being slighted, is met by a soft answer that turns away wrath — Scripture commends sharp rebuke aimed at doctrinal health while commending gentleness in the face of sharpness aimed merely at personal honor.
roots_summary: Sharply's root sense (scearp, an edge that cuts) is applied consistently across Scripture to speech, whether the sharpness is a fault, as in Ephraim's wounded pride, or a pastoral duty, as in Paul's charge to Titus, the moral weight determined entirely by the speaker's aim, not the sharpness itself.
roots_lines: Sharply in Judges 8 describes Ephraim's aggrieved chiding of Gideon over being excluded from battle.
Gideon answers their sharpness not in kind but with a soft, honor-deflecting reply.
Sharply in Titus 1 commands Titus to rebuke false teachers plainly, for the church's doctrinal health.
Paul specifies the purpose: that they may be sound in the faith, sharpness aimed at healing, not wounding.
The same word thus names both a fault of wounded pride and a duty of pastoral care, depending on its aim.
usage: They did chide with him sharply — Ephraim's wounded-pride complaint against Gideon.
Gideon's soft answer turns away wrath — a contrasting response to sharpness born of pride (cf. Prov 15:1).
Rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith — Paul's charge to Titus regarding false teachers.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon sceort (short) — comparative degree, of less length; applied in the Authorized Version to both a proverbial bed too small to stretch on and the architecture of Ezekiel's temple vision.
biblical_def:
The bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it. The upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these.

Shorter measures inadequacy in one place and deliberate proportion in the other. Isaiah's brief, memorable proverb pictures false security as a bed too short to lie on and a covering too narrow to wrap in — every human attempt to find safety apart from the LORD reduced to furniture that cannot do the one thing furniture is for. The image lands its blow precisely because it is so ordinary: not cosmic catastrophe but a bed that simply does not fit. Ezekiel's temple vision uses the same comparative word with none of that irony — the upper chambers were shorter than the lower by design, part of a structure measured with total precision, the shortening itself functional and intended rather than a failure. One shorter names something too small for the purpose it was meant to serve; the other names a chamber exactly the size its purpose required.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SHORT: not long; not extended in length; comparative degree, applied to a bed too small in Isaiah's proverb and to chamber dimensions in Ezekiel's temple vision.
webster_full: SHORT, a. Not long; not extended in measure or duration.
SHORT, a. Insufficient; not adequate to the purpose intended.
SHORTER, a. The comparative degree of short; of less length or extent.
In Isaiah 28 the word pictures false security as a bed too short to serve its purpose.
In Ezekiel 42 the word describes the temple's upper chambers, shorter than the lower by design.
scriptures: For the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it.
Eze 42:5
Now the upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these, than the lower, and than the middlemost of the building.
corruption_summary: Reading Isaiah's short-bed proverb as generic wisdom about unmet expectations, detached from its specific target — Judah's covenant with death and hell, their refuge of lies (Isa 28:15, 17-18) — loses the sharp edge of a warning against trusting political alliance rather than the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: A generalized moral reading treats the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it as universal wisdom about disappointment, detached from its immediate target: Judah's leaders had made a covenant with death, a false alliance meant to secure the nation against Assyria apart from trusting the LORD. Isaiah's proverb names that alliance specifically as furniture too small to actually protect anyone who lies down on it.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Ezekiel 42's contrasting use of the same comparative: a shorter dimension is not always inadequacy, but can be precise, intentional design — the LORD's own house measured to the cubit, every proportion, tall and short alike, exactly as the architect ordained.
roots_summary: Isaiah's short-bed proverb and Ezekiel's temple measurements use the identical comparative form for opposite purposes, one exposing a false refuge's inadequacy, the other displaying the LORD's own exacting architectural design, the word itself morally neutral until its context supplies the judgment.
roots_lines: Shorter in Isaiah 28 pictures false security as furniture inadequate to its purpose, too small to rest on.
The proverb targets specifically Judah's covenant with death, an alliance apart from trusting the LORD.
Shorter in Ezekiel 42 describes the temple's upper chambers, shorter than the lower by deliberate design.
The temple vision's precision (measured with a measuring reed) frames shortness there as intentional, not deficient.
The same comparative word thus serves both warning (Isaiah) and architectural precision (Ezekiel).
usage: The bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it — false security exposed as inadequate.
The covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it — the proverb's parallel image of exposure.
The upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these — precise temple architecture.

etymology: Anglo-Saxon sona (immediately, soon) — comparative degree, of less time elapsed; used in the Authorized Version both of a longed-for restoration and of the sun's swift, withering heat.
biblical_def:
That I may be restored to you the sooner. The sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass.

Sooner marks two very different kinds of speed. Hebrews closes its letter with a personal request, asking for prayer that I may be restored to you the sooner — an ordinary, affectionate desire for a reunion to come quickly, the writer's ministry bound up in real relationship with real people he misses. James uses the identical comparative for something far less welcome: the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, the swiftness this time a warning, the rich man's fading glory pictured as grass scorched almost the instant the sun appears, gone before it is fairly noticed. One sooner is prayed for as a blessing; the other arrives, uninvited, as a judgment on riches trusted rather than held loosely — both, in their own way, teaching that time in Scripture is never neutral, but always moving toward an end that matters.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SOON: in a short time; without delay; comparative degree, of less time elapsed than expected or than another event.
webster_full: SOON, adv. Before long; shortly after any time specified or supposed.
SOON, adv. Without delay; forthwith; early.
SOONER, adv. The comparative degree of soon; in less time; more quickly.
In Hebrews 13 the word expresses a personal hope for a quicker reunion, in prayer.
In James 1 the word describes the sun's swift, withering effect on grass, a figure for fading riches.
scriptures: But I beseech you the rather to do this, that I may be restored to you the sooner.
Jas 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
corruption_summary: A prosperity-gospel framing that treats material riches as an unqualified sign of blessing runs directly against James's own figure: the rich man's glory fades no sooner than grass under a burning sun, riches offering no more permanence than the flower James pictures falling in the same breath.
corruption_paragraphs: Teaching that equates wealth automatically with divine favor, without qualification, cannot easily accommodate James 1:11's blunt comparison: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways, riches given the same brief, scorched lifespan as grass under a rising sun. James is not condemning riches as such but the false security placed in them, a security that vanishes exactly as fast as the vegetation his figure describes.

Beyond the point above, this entry faces no further significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Hebrews 13's own warmer use of the same comparative: sooner is not always a word of warning; the writer's plea to be restored to you the sooner shows that ordinary Christian affection, and longing for reunion with fellow believers, is itself a legitimate object of prayer, not a lesser concern beneath doctrinal or pastoral business.
roots_summary: Sooner's two occurrences frame the comparative at opposite emotional poles — a personal hope prayed for in Hebrews, a sober warning pictured in James — the shared Anglo-Saxon root (sona, soon) carrying both without needing separate words for each.
roots_lines: Sooner in Hebrews 13 expresses the writer's personal hope for a quicker reunion with those he addresses.
The request is framed as a matter for prayer, tying ordinary affection to the church's spiritual life.
Sooner in James 1 describes the sun's swift, withering effect on grass, a figure for fading riches.
James applies the figure directly: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
The same comparative word thus serves both a warm personal hope and a sober warning against riches.
usage: That I may be restored to you the sooner — a personal hope for reunion, offered as a matter for prayer.
The sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass — riches' brief, scorched lifespan.
So also shall the rich man fade away in his ways — James's direct application of the figure.
